name: Critical and Sensitive Periods
what: This subtopic examines the role of maturation and brain plasticity in determining windows of opportunity for skill acquisition. It distinguishes between critical periods, in which a skill must be acquired within a set window or may never develop, and sensitive periods, in which a skill is most efficiently acquired but can still develop later.
why: Understanding critical and sensitive periods explains why early childhood experiences have such a profound and sometimes irreversible impact on development. This knowledge is also directly relevant to the case study of Genie, which provides evidence for and against the critical period hypothesis.

items.title: I can define maturation and explain how it determines the timing of development
items.what: Maturation is the biologically programmed process of growth that follows a fixed sequence and facilitates all aspects of development. Each individual has a unique developmental map determined at conception that sets out when specific developmental events will occur.
items.why: Maturation is the biological mechanism underlying both critical and sensitive periods, connecting this subtopic to the broader theme of nature and biological factors in development.
items.example: All children follow the same broad sequence of motor development, sitting before standing before walking, but the exact age at which each milestone occurs varies between individuals based on their unique maturation trajectory.

items.title: I can define brain plasticity and explain why it is higher during infancy and childhood
items.what: Brain plasticity is the brain's ability to physically change its structure in response to experience and learning. Plasticity is highest during infancy and early childhood because the brain is more malleable at this stage, allowing new pathways to form and strengthen more readily than in adulthood.
items.why: Plasticity is the neurological basis for why early experiences have such a strong influence on development and why critical and sensitive periods are concentrated in early life.
items.example: A child learning a second language at age 5 acquires it with native-like fluency because their brain readily forms the neural pathways required for the new language. An adult learning the same language must work against a less malleable brain, making the process slower and less complete.

items.title: I can define critical periods and explain what happens if the skill is not acquired within the window
items.what: A critical period is a narrow, rigid developmental window in which a specific function or skill must be acquired. If the skill is not acquired during this window, it may never fully develop or may remain severely impaired regardless of later exposure.
items.why: Critical periods represent some of the most significant and irreversible effects of the environment on development, making them important for understanding cases of extreme deprivation and the limits of later remediation.
items.example: First-language acquisition has a critical period roughly between birth and 5 years. Genie, who was isolated until age 13.5 and never spoken to, was later unable to fully develop grammar or verbal sentence production, suggesting these aspects of language had critical periods she had passed.

items.title: I can define sensitive periods and explain how they differ from critical periods
items.what: A sensitive period is the optimal developmental window for acquiring a skill in the fastest and most efficient way. Unlike critical periods, missing a sensitive period does not prevent the skill from developing; it simply means the process will be slower and more effortful, and the eventual level of mastery may be lower.
items.why: Distinguishing between critical and sensitive periods is a precise skill tested in both multiple-choice and short-answer questions, particularly around the use of words like 'must' versus 'optimally'.
items.example: Second-language acquisition has a sensitive period up to approximately age 12. A person who begins learning Italian at age 30 can still become proficient, but is unlikely to achieve native-speaker fluency in grammar and accent compared to someone who began as a child.

items.title: I can use the case study of Genie to evaluate the critical period hypothesis for language acquisition
items.what: The critical period hypothesis proposes that first-language acquisition must occur within a set developmental window or will not fully develop. Genie's case provides partial support: she could not develop grammar or produce verbal sentences after her critical period had passed, but she was able to learn individual words, suggesting some aspects of language have critical periods while others have sensitive periods.
items.why: Genie's case is the primary real-world evidence for discussing the critical period hypothesis in VCE Psychology and is commonly used in exam questions requiring students to both describe findings and evaluate a hypothesis.
items.example: Genie acquired a vocabulary of single words and two-word combinations after intervention, which suggests word learning does not have a strict critical period. However, her permanent inability to produce full sentences or understand intonation suggests these skills do have critical periods that had passed before she received language exposure.

items.title: I can compare critical and sensitive periods using a specific example of each
items.what: Critical periods are narrow, begin and end abruptly, and relate to skills that must be acquired within the window. Sensitive periods are broader, begin and end more gradually, and relate to skills that are simply easiest to acquire during the window but can still develop later.
items.why: Comparison questions requiring students to use both definitions alongside examples are a common exam format and require precise use of language, particularly 'must' for critical periods and 'optimal' for sensitive periods.
items.example: First-language grammar acquisition (critical period, roughly 0-5 years) must occur within the window or the skill may be permanently impaired, as seen in Genie. Second-language acquisition (sensitive period, roughly up to age 12) is most efficient in childhood, but Asanka, who began learning Spanish at 21, can still acquire it, just more slowly and with less likely fluency.
